gap: Character fidelity at medium-close-up range. Pass only if all of these are visible in the frame: hair broken into strands or clumps with a soft, non-solid edge against the background; a face with skin micro-variation, defined eyes and brows and a readable expression; skin whose specular varies, with no uniform plastic sheen on the forearms; at least several readable cloth folds at the shoulders, elbows and waist, with seams and contact shadows; and a held pose with intent (gripping or bracing a prop) instead of a default arms-down idle. The head-and-torso framing should fill at least about 70% of the frame height.

Encoded footage: /private/tmp/opus55/critic/on-foot-C2/onfoot/onfoot_footage.mp4 and /private/tmp/opus55/critic/on-foot-C2/route/route_footage.mp4.. Judge: The more polished image wins decisively in all four pairs. None of the losses is close, and none is indistinguishable. In three pairs (1-3) the winner is A; in pair 4 it is B. All four losing frames look like they come from the same in-development city game, a Singapore-like setting with a recurring olive-shirt protagonist. Its one consistent strength is warm low-sun lighting with long, soft shadows, and in places it does read as a real location (HDB blocks with void decks, shophouse colonnades). It loses for the same reasons every time. First, character fidelity: helmet-like hair, a waxy, expressionless face, flat cloth and a stiff default idle or gait. Second, life and density: empty plazas and streets with almost no pedestrians or traffic. Third, material and set-dressing sterility: one repeating paver texture dominates every frame, with no wear, clutter or props, and there are placeholder tells such as a blank sign and primitive blocks. Fourth, weak cinematic intent: the subject is centered or small, the compositions are static, and the landmark backdrops have no aerial perspective. The winning frames set a bar close to key art, with storytelling props, layered foreground-to-background depth, readable faces and crowded, busy streets. One of them carries a logo overlay, so they are curated marketing shots and not raw gameplay. The quickest gains for the in-development game would be populating streets with pedestrians and traffic, and upgrading the hero character's hair, skin and cloth shading. Breaking up the paver tiling and adding set dressing would come next. Only two winning frames genuinely wowed: the walk away from the burning truck and the crowded neon night street.
